outcomes: Read training and validation learning curves together
lessons: When a correct gradient still fails

learning-curve.name: Learning curve
learning-curve.definition: A sequence of measured losses or metrics recorded as training progresses.
learning-curve.explanation: A training curve shows how well parameters fit the examples used for updates. A validation curve measures the same checkpoints on held-out examples. Reading them together separates optimization trouble from generalization trouble: both remaining high suggests poor optimization or an inadequate model, while training improving as validation worsens suggests overfitting. Curves depend on the measurement interval and reduction convention. They are evidence from one run, not a guarantee about every random seed or dataset.

minibatch.name: Minibatch
minibatch.definition: A subset of training examples used to estimate one parameter update.
minibatch.explanation: A full-batch gradient averages every training example before each update. A minibatch uses fewer examples, reducing the work per update and introducing variation because different batches produce different estimates. Batch size changes both computation and optimization behavior. This chapter uses fixed ordered chunks for a deterministic teaching trace. Production stochastic training typically shuffles training examples between epochs so persistent order patterns do not bias consecutive updates.

regularization.name: Regularization
regularization.definition: A modification intended to favor models that transfer better to unseen data.
regularization.explanation: L2 regularization adds lambda times the squared weights to the training objective. Its derivative adds 2 lambda w to each weight gradient, pulling large weights toward zero. The bias is left unpenalized in this chapter. Regularization deliberately accepts some training error when that restriction improves held-out behavior. Lambda is a hyperparameter selected on validation evidence. A regularizer does not repair leakage, unrepresentative data, or an incorrectly defined target.

generalization.name: Generalization
generalization.definition: Useful performance on relevant examples that were not used to fit the model.
generalization.explanation: Training minimizes an empirical objective on observed samples, but the real aim is usually performance on future data from the intended setting. A validation or test split provides an estimate of this transfer under assumptions about how the samples were collected. Generalization is not simply low training loss, and a synthetic held-out result does not establish real-world reliability. Model capacity, data quantity, noise, regularization, and distribution shift all affect the gap.
